{{Short description|Constitutive relation}}

In theoretical [[glaciology]] and [[continuum mechanics]], the '''Glen–Nye flow law''', also referred to as '''Glen's flow law''', is an empirically derived [[constitutive relation]] widely used as a model for the [[rheology]] of [[glacial ice]].<ref name="CuffeyPatterson2010">{{cite book |last1=Cuffey |first1=K. |first2=W. S. B. |last2=Paterson |title=The Physics of Glaciers |date=2010 |page=55, 60 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=9780123694614 |edition=4}}</ref> The Glen–Nye flow law treats ice as a purely [[viscous]], [[Incompressible flow|incompressible]], [[isotropy#Physics|isotropic]], [[non-Newtonian fluid]], with a viscosity determined by a [[Power-law#Power-law functions|power law]] relation between [[strain rate]] and [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]]:<ref name="Glenn1952">{{cite journal |last1=Glen |first1=J. W. |title=Experiments on the deformation of ice |journal=Journal of Glaciology |date=1952 |volume=2 |issue=12 |pages=111–114 |doi=10.3189/S0022143000034067|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Nye1953">{{cite journal |last1=Nye |first1=J. F. |title=The flow law of ice from measurements in glacier tunnels, laboratory experiments and the Jungfraufirn borehole experiment |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A |date=1953 |volume=219 |issue=1139 |pages=477–489 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1953.0161}}</ref> 

<math display="block">\dot{\epsilon}_{e} = A\tau^{n}_e</math>

The effective strain rate <math>\dot{\epsilon}_{e}</math> (units of [[Inverse second|s<sup>−1</sup>]]) and effective stress <math>\tau_e</math> (units of [[Pascal (unit)|Pa]]) are related to the second [[Invariants of tensors|principle invariants]] of their respective [[tensors]].<ref name="Nye1953" /> The parameters <math>A</math> and <math>n</math> are scalar constants which have been estimated through a combination of theory and measurements. The exponent <math>n</math> is dimensionless, and the rate factor <math>A</math> takes on the units Pa<sup>−<math>n</math></sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. The Glen–Nye flow law simplifies the [[viscous stress tensor]] to a single scalar value <math>\mu</math>, the [[dynamic viscosity]], which is determined by [[tensor invariants]] of the [[Cauchy stress tensor#Stress deviator tensor|deviatoric stress tensor]] <math>\boldsymbol\tau</math> and the [[strain rate tensor]] <math>\boldsymbol \dot{\epsilon}</math>.

Under the application of sustained force ice will flow as a fluid, and changes to the force applied will result in non-linear changes to the resulting flow.<ref name="Glenn1955" /> This fluid behavior of ice, which the Glen–Nye flow law is intended to represent, is accommodated within the solid ice by [[Creep (deformation)|creep]],<ref name="Glenn1955">{{cite journal |last1=Glen |first1=J. W. |title=The creep of polycrystalline ice |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A |date=1955 |volume=228 |issue=1175 |pages=519–538 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1955.0066}}</ref> and is a dominant mode of glacial [[ice flow]].<ref name="Forbes1846">{{cite journal |last1=Forbes |first1=James D. |title=Illustrations of the viscous theory of glacier motion |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society |date=1846 |volume=136 |pages=143–210 |doi=10.1098/rstl.1846.0013}}</ref><ref name="Nye1953" />{{sfn|Cuffey|Paterson|2010|p=29}}

==Viscosity definition==
The constitutive relation is developed as a [[generalized Newtonian fluid]], where the deviatoric stress and strain tensors are related by a viscosity scalar:

{{Equation box 1
|indent=:
|title='''Glen–Nye [[constitutive law]]  of ice''' 
|equation=<math>\boldsymbol\tau=2\mu\dot{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}</math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #000000
|background colour = #DCDCDC
}}

where <math>\mu</math> is the viscosity (units of Pa s), <math>\boldsymbol\tau</math> is the deviatoric stress tensor, and <math>\boldsymbol \dot{\epsilon}</math> is the strain rate tensor. In some derivations, <math>\lambda=(2\mu)^{-1}</math> (units of Pa<sup>−1</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>) is substituted.<ref name="Nye1953" />

This construction makes several assumptions:<ref name="Nye1953" /><ref name="Glen1958">{{cite journal |last1=Glen |first1=J. W. |title=The flow law of ice: A discussion of the assumptions made in glacier theory, their experimental foundations and consequences |journal=IUGG/IAHS Symp. Of Chamonix, IAHS Publ. |date=1958 |volume=47 |pages=171–183 |url=https://iahs.info/uploads/dms/04719.pdf |access-date=2024-01-27 |archive-date=2024-01-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240127214846/https://iahs.info/uploads/dms/04719.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

* [[Isotropy]], as the single proportionality scalar is the same for all tensor components.
* [[Incompressible flow|Incompressibility]], as volumetric stress is ignored and only the deviatoric stress can do work. 
* That corresponding components of the two tensors are directly proportional to one another, i.e. <math>\tau_{ij} \propto \dot{\epsilon}_{ij}</math>. Theoretically, this assumption results from ignoring the third principle invariant of the tensors; physically, this means that the strain rate can only change along the same axes as the [[Cauchy stress tensor#Principal stresses and stress invariants|principal stresses]].

While incompressibility is an accurate assumption for glacial ice, glacial ice can be anisotropic and in general the strain rate may respond perpendicularly to the principal stress.<ref name="Glen1958" /><ref name="VanDerVeen1990" />

''With these assumptions, the stress and strain rate tensors here are symmetric and have a trace of zero, properties that allow their invariants and squares to be simplified from the general definitions.''

The deviatoric stress tensor is related to an [[effective stress]] by its second principal invariant:<ref name="Nye1953" />
:<math>\tau_e^2 = II_{\boldsymbol{\tau}} = \frac{1}{2}\tau_{ij} \tau_{ij}</math>

where [[Einstein notation]] implies summation over repeated indices. 

The same is defined for an effective strain rate:<ref name="Nye1953" />
:<math>\dot{\epsilon}_e^2 = II_{\boldsymbol{\dot{\epsilon}}} = \frac{1}{2}\dot{\epsilon}_{ij} \dot{\epsilon}_{ij}</math>

From this form, we can recognize that:
:<math> \boldsymbol\tau^2 = \tau_{ij} \tau_{ij} =2\tau_e^2</math>
and 
:<math> \boldsymbol{\dot{\epsilon}}^2 = \dot{\epsilon}_{ij} \dot{\epsilon}_{ij} =2\dot{\epsilon}_e^2 </math>

The viscosity is scalar and cannot be negative (a fluid cannot gain energy as it flows), so <math>\mu</math> can be expressed in terms of the invariant effective stress and effective strain rate.

<math display="block">
\mu= \frac{\boldsymbol{\tau}}{2\dot{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}}=\frac{1}{2} \tau_e \dot{\epsilon}_e^{-1}  
</math>

Here, the Glen–Nye flow law allows us to substitute for either <math>\tau_e</math> or <math>\dot{\epsilon}_e</math>, and <math>\mu</math> can be defined in terms of either the effective strain rate or effective stress alone:

{{Equation box 1
|indent=:
|title='''Glen–Nye [[viscosity]] of ice''' 
|equation=<math>\mu=\frac{A^{-1/n}}{2 \dot{\epsilon}_e^{(n-1)/n}} = \frac{\tau_e^{(1-n)}}{2A}
</math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #000000
|background colour = #DCDCDC
}}

where <math>B=A^{-1/n}</math> (units of Pa s<math>^{1/n}</math>) is sometimes substituted.<ref name="Nye1953" /><ref name="Glenn1955" />

==Parameter values==
The Glen–Nye rheology model defines two parameters, <math>A</math> and <math>n</math>. 

The rate factor <math>A</math> has been found empirically to vary with temperature and is often modeled with an [[Arrhenius equation|Arrhenius relation]] describing the [[Creep (deformation)#Temperature dependence|temperature dependence of creep]]:<ref name="Glenn1955" /><ref name="VanDerVeen1990">{{cite journal |last1=Van Der Veen |first1=Cornelis J. |last2=Whillans |first2=I. M.  |title=Flow laws for glacier ice: comparison of numerical predictions and field measurements |journal=Journal of Glaciology |date=1990 |volume=36 |issue=124 |pages=324–339|doi=10.3189/002214390793701372 |hdl=1808/17348 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
:<math>A=A_0 e^{(-Q/RT)}</math>
where <math>Q</math> is the [[activation energy]], <math>R</math> is the [[universal gas constant]], and <math>T</math> is the [[absolute temperature]]. The prefactor <math>A_0</math> may be dependent on [[crystal structure]], impurities, damage, or other qualities of the ice.<ref name="VanDerVeen1990" /> Estimates of <math>A</math> vary by orders of magnitude and can be derived as a single value from an estimated value for <math>A_0</math>, or by comparing measurements of multiple real world glaciers and experiments,<ref name="CuffeyPatterson2010" /> or treated as a [[scalar field]] inferred from observations by a [[inverse problem|numerical inversion]] of the [[Cauchy momentum equation|momentum equation]] for ice flow at a specific location.<ref name="Larour2005">{{cite journal |last1=Larour |first1=E. |last2=Rignot |first2=E. |last3=Joughin |first3=I. |last4=Aubry |first4=D. |title=Rheology of the Ronne Ice Shelf, Antarctica, inferred from satellite radar interferometry data using an inverse control method |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |date=2005 |volume=32 |issue=5 |doi=10.1029/2004GL021693}}</ref>

Viscous ice flow is an example of [[shear thinning]], which corresponds to <math>n>1</math>. Review of research using a variety of methods and field sites have found the range of plausible values to be around <math>2<n<4</math> with the most commonly used assumption to be a constant <math>n=3</math>.<ref name="CuffeyPatterson2010" /> However, the value of <math>n</math> is also stress dependent, and can reflect different microstructural mechanisms facilitating creep at different stress regimes.<ref name="Goldsby2001">{{cite journal |last1=Goldsby |first1=D. |last2=Kohlstedt |first2=D. L. |title=Superplastic deformation of ice: Experimental observations |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |date=2001 |volume=106 |pages=11017–11030|doi=10.1029/2000JB900336 }}</ref>

Methods to improve estimations of these viscous parameters are an ongoing field of research.<ref name="Millstein2022">{{cite journal |last1=Millstein |first1= J.D. |last2=Minchew |first2=B.M. |last3=Pegler |first3=S.S. |title=Ice viscosity is more sensitive to stress than commonly assumed |journal=Communications Earth and Environment |date=2022 |volume=3 |issue=57 |doi=10.1038/s43247-022-00385-x |doi-access=free|hdl=1912/29119 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Wang2022">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yongji |first2=Ching-Yao |last2=Lai |first3=Charlie |last3=Cowen-Breen |title=Discovering the rheology of Antarctic Ice Shelves via physics-informed deep learning |journal=(Preprint) |date=2022 |url=https://assets.researchsquare.com/files/rs-2135795/v1/1c0f344eb9b7ef8a61058ad8.pdf?c=1669779218 |access-date=2024-01-27 |archive-date=2023-06-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230615142051/https://assets.researchsquare.com/files/rs-2135795/v1/1c0f344eb9b7ef8a61058ad8.pdf?c=1669779218 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Limitations==
The use of the word "law" in referring to the Glen-Nye model of ice rheology may obscure the complexity of factors which determine the range of viscous ice flow parameter values even within a single glacier, as well as the significant assumptions and simplifications made by the model itself.{{sfn|Cuffey|Paterson|2010|p=55}}<ref name="Paterson1983">{{cite journal |last1=Paterson |first1=W. S. B. |title=Deformation within polar ice sheets: an analysis of the Byrd Station and Camp Century borehole-tilting measurements |journal=Cold Regions Science and Technology |date=1983 |volume=8 |issue=2 |doi=10.1016/0165-232X(83)90007-1 |pages=165–179}}</ref><ref name="Glen1958" /> 

In particular, treatment of the ice as a fluid with bulk properties does not represent and may struggle to capture the cascade of mechanisms which allow the ice to deform at the grain scale in solid state.{{sfn|Cuffey|Paterson|2010|p=51}}<ref name="Goldsby2001" /> Glacial ice crystals grow on scales of millimeters up to 10 cm,{{sfn|Cuffey|Paterson|2010|p=69}}<ref name="Seligman1949">{{cite journal |last1=Seligman |first1=Gerald |title=The growth of the glacier crystal |journal=Journal of Glaciology |date=1949 |volume=1 |issue=5 |pages=254–268 |doi=10.3189/002214349793702601}}</ref> and constant readjustment between grain structure and internal stress results in high variations in strain across the same length-scale as the crystals themselves.<ref name="Faria2014">{{cite journal |last1=Faria |first1=Sérgio H. |last2=Weikusat |first2=Ilka |last3= Azuma |first3=Nobuhiko   |title=The microstructure of polar ice. Part II: State of the art |journal=Journal of Structural Geology |date=2014 |volume=61 |pages=21–49 |doi=10.1016/j.jsg.2013.11.003|url=https://epic.awi.de/id/eprint/35371/1/FariaEA2013_PartII_accepted_JournalStructGeol.pdf }}</ref> Additionally, individual ice crystals are not isotropic,<ref name="Faria2014" /> and typically are not randomly oriented within the material fabric which undergoes [[dynamic recrystallization]].<ref name="Duval 1995">{{cite journal |last1=P. Duval, O. Castelnau |title=Dynamic Recrystallization of Ice in Polar Ice Sheets |journal=Journal de Physique IV |date=1995 |volume=5 |issue=C3 |pages=197–205 |doi=10.1051/jp4:1995317|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/jpa-00253683/file/ajp-jp4199505C317.pdf }}</ref> Grain size and fabric orientation are known to influence the creep of glacial ice, but are dynamic properties which also evolve with the stress regime and are not simple to capture in a model.{{sfn|Cuffey|Paterson|2010|p=66, 72}}

The Glen-Nye flow law also does not render the full range of ice response to stress, including [[elastic deformation]], [[fracture mechanics]] (i.e. [[crevasses]]), and transient phases of creep.{{sfn|Cuffey|Paterson|2010|p=29}}<ref name="Glenn1952" />
